questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a cable did to the distance between orders
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a submarine cable changed decision-making at a distance
questions.stem: Explain how a submarine cable changed the distance between orders, and why that change mattered more than the speed of any single message.

answer.exemplar: Before the cable, an order travelled at the speed of a steamer, and a dispatch from one capital to another might take a fortnight to arrive and the same time to be acted on, so war and government proceeded at postal pace. A working cable carried a message in minutes and the reply in minutes, but the decisive effect was not the speed of the traffic itself: it was that decision and action became continuous, because no commander had to choose between acting on stale information and waiting. Distances that had been measured in weeks were re-expressed as a single working day.

questions.explanation: The cable mattered because it removed the lag between decision and action, so distance became hours rather than weeks. Faster messages alone miss that the constraint was the round trip.
questions.hint: Ask what commanders could do that they could not do before.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A fort that priced a river instead of closing it
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a fortress could tax a river rather than close it
questions.stem: Explain how a fortress on a river could serve a state by taxing passage rather than by closing the waterway, and why the choice between those two uses was made on revenue grounds.

answer.exemplar: A fortress placed where a river narrowed could bar shipping entirely, and a state that did so would destroy the trade passing along it as well as any rival's use of the route. The same fort could instead be staffed by collectors who let vessels pass after payment, and it then became a source of revenue rather than a barrier, and a reason for travellers to route their business through that state's territory. The decision therefore turned on the relative value of the customs income against the value of the trade that a closure would have driven away, and rulers moved between the two policies as circumstances changed.

questions.explanation: Closing the river forbade passage but destroyed the traffic that paid the tolls, so one fort could be a customs point or a barrier by revenue. A permanently military purpose ignores the arithmetic of the trade.
questions.hint: Ask what a closure would cost the state.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a defensive weapon changed the value of ground
questions.learningObjective: Explain what rapid fire did to ground and to the conduct of war
questions.stem: Explain why a rapid-fire weapon changed the value of ground, and why the change did not settle every question about how such a war would be fought.

answer.exemplar: A weapon that could fire many rounds without the long recovery of a muzzle-loading gun made the approach across open ground suicidal for anyone who could not answer it with equal fire, so the side holding prepared positions could dictate the terms of contact. That much shifted the value of ground towards the defender and made the direct assault almost a memory of older wars. What it did not settle was the larger question of movement: forces that dispersed, avoided fixed lines and used the country to turn the enemy's fire on itself could still bring the war to a decision, and the campaigns in which the new weapon appeared are remembered precisely for such indirect methods.

questions.explanation: A rapid-fire weapon made prepared positions decisive in the front line, so ground held value and open attacks did not, yet dispersion and mobility could defeat it. It did not decide the war alone.
questions.hint: Ask what a prepared position was worth.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: How coaling stations set a fleet's reach
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a depot network determined a fleet's reach
questions.stem: Explain how a network of coaling stations determined the reach of a fleet, and why the geography of the depots mattered as much as the coal they held.

answer.exemplar: A steamship squadron could not stay at sea longer than its bunkers lasted, and could not go on long without topping them up somewhere, so the reach of a fleet was the reach of its depots plus the distance a ship could steam on a full load. That made the possession of a coaling station a reason to wish for the harbour where it stood, whether for the coal itself or for the shelter it gave while filling, and it gave a state that wanted to operate far from its own shores a reason to acquire or keep such places. Geography mattered as much as stores, because a station in the wrong strait or the wrong ocean was of little use to a fleet steaming in the other direction.

questions.explanation: A fleet's endurance was its bunkers plus the distance to the next depot, so the map of depots was the map of its operations. Coal alone does not set reach, because where the stations lay decides too.
questions.hint: Ask where the ship had to go next.

answer.exemplar: A company that raised regiments, manned forts and fought for its trading privileges was exercising the public power of defence without bearing the public cost, and it did so in places where the state had little reach of its own. questions.topic: What a prophylactic changed about the campaigning season
questions.learningObjective: Explain why prophylaxis changed the campaigning season
questions.stem: Explain how a prophylactic medicine changed the campaigning season, and why doctors did not at first regard the change as a settled improvement.

answer.exemplar: For most of the nineteenth century the season in which troops could be kept in the field was set by the months of fever, because the men were simply unable to march and fight through them. When quinine began to be taken as a matter of routine rather than as a remedy after the first attack, the fever season ceased to be a closed barrier, and campaigns that had waited for the cool months could be planned for the hot ones. answer.exemplar: At a frontier the trader might have to state a quantity twice: once in the measures of the trading nation and once in those of the district, and a customs officer would have to accept a statement given in a language he did not read. That arrangement had the advantage of letting each side keep the habits of its own trade, but it also meant that the terms of the bargain were settled twice, in two systems of measurement and two sets of words, and each system could be stretched in its own direction. questions.topic: What a trade grant converted a market into
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a trade grant opened a market
questions.stem: Explain how a trade grant converted a restricted market into an open one, and why the terms of the grant mattered more than its generosity.

answer.exemplar: A market restricted by a single port, a single company or a monopoly of its own traders could be opened by granting outsiders access on stated terms: ports designated, duties fixed, goods admitted, and disputes settled by a known procedure. The value of such a grant lay less in the favour shown to foreign traders than in the certainty it gave them, because a merchant who knows the duty in advance can price his goods and compete, whereas one subject to discretion at every port cannot. questions.topic: How coaling stations set a fleet's reach

stimulus.body: The minute records that the fleet's colliers have been laid up and that oil is now taken in their place from tankers sent out to meet the squadron, and that the men are no longer able to replenish at the coaling stations, which cannot supply the new fuel. It notes that the squadrons must now be kept within reach of the sea where the tankers can reach them.

questions.stem: Given the minute, what has changed for the fleet's reach?

options.text: That the limit is now set by where tankers can reach the fleet, rather than by where coal was stored
That the fleet can stay at sea indefinitely, since tankers carry more fuel than colliers did
options.misconception: claims the change removed all limits

options.text: That the coaling stations have been converted to store oil instead of coal
options.misconception: invents a conversion of the depots

options.text: That the fleet's size has been reduced, since fewer ships can be supplied at sea
options.misconception: invents a change in fleet size

questions.explanation: The minute says the old stations cannot supply the new fuel, so the fleet is bound by the reach of the tankers and no longer counts on its depots. The alternatives claim the limit vanished or the depots changed use.
questions.hint: Ask what the stations could not do.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a cable did to the distance between orders
questions.learningObjective: Compare the reach of a cable across groups in society
questions.stem: A cable company's seminar asks what a working cable changed about the world its subscribers lived in. Compare the effect on governments, on markets and on the family.

options.text: The cable mattered only to governments, since families still waited for letters
options.misconception: denies the effect on households

options.text: The cable shrank the interval in which news travelled, for governments, markets and households alike
The cable increased the volume of traffic without changing the time messages took
options.misconception: confuses volume with speed

options.text: The cable widened the gap between those who could afford it and those who could not
options.misconception: makes the effect one of exclusion

questions.explanation: One change in transmission speed re-ordered government, commerce and household knowledge alike. The alternatives isolate one group, confuse volume with speed or claim the effect was exclusion.
questions.hint: Ask which intervals the cable governed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a prophylactic changed about the campaigning season
questions.learningObjective: Read a chart of campaigning months across years
questions.stem: A chart plots, for each campaign of the decade, the months of the year during which the column was in the field. What does the widening of the bars show?

options.text: That the campaigns were planned in ignorance of the medical advice they received
options.misconception: claims the medical advice was ignored

options.text: That the months of fever ceased to close the campaigning season as the practice became routine
That the army's strength grew steadily, since more men were present in later campaigns
options.misconception: reads the chart as a strength series

options.text: That the routes grew shorter, so that campaigns took fewer months each year
options.misconception: infers shorter routes from the chart

questions.explanation: Longer bars show campaigns spreading into months previously closed by fever, so the season lengthened as prevention became routine. The alternatives read advice, strength or routes into a timing chart.
questions.hint: Ask what made the bars longer.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a defensive weapon changed the value of ground
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the effect of the rifle from that of the machine gun
questions.stem: Explain how the spread of the repeating rifle and then of the machine gun changed what infantry could achieve, and why the two changes are often confused with each other.

answer.exemplar: The rifled musket gave a soldier a weapon whose aim and range were his own rather than his company's, so the massed volley of an earlier age gave way to aimed fire and the casualty of an advance climbed steeply. The machine gun then made the supply of that aimed fire almost unlimited within its range, so a defended position could deliver a volume of bullets that an attack could not answer. Historians often run the two changes together, yet they belong to different moments and had different consequences: the rifle made fire effective at long range, while the machine gun made fire continuous and abundant, and it was the second that turned ground into something to be held rather than something to be crossed.

questions.explanation: The rifle gave aimed fire at range and the machine gun made fire abundant and continuous, and the second turned ground into something held rather than crossed. Merging them hides which change produced the trench.
questions.hint: Ask which weapon supplied volume of fire.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a trade grant converted a market into
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish what a grant settled from what it fixed

stimulus.body: The foreign representatives are permitted to reside at the open ports and to trade there; the government of Japan engages to give full protection to persons and property sojourning at those ports; and the tariffs are to be published and to remain unaltered for the term of twenty years, subject to the consent of the parties.

questions.stem: According to the article, what did the grant settle and leave open?

options.text: It settled the terms of access and protection, but left the level of duties fixed for twenty years
options.misconception: reads the tariff clause as a matter of access alone

options.text: It settled access, protection and the tariff, though the tariff could not change for twenty years
It settled nothing beyond the choice of ports, leaving duties and protection to be fixed later
options.misconception: ignores the protection clause

options.text: It fixed the duties permanently, and made the consent of the parties unnecessary
options.misconception: overreads the twenty-year clause

questions.explanation: The article covers residence and trade, protection of persons and property, and a published tariff unalterable for twenty years without consent. The alternatives treat the tariff as untouched or the protection clause as absent.
questions.hint: Ask which article fixes a price.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A company's armed force and the state's bill
questions.learningObjective: Assess who bore the cost of a company's armies

stimulus.body: The report states that the company's armies in India are maintained at a cost which the revenues of the territories under its rule have more than covered in most years, and that the company has not called upon the government for money since the charter of 1813. It further states that the company remains under the obligation of providing for the defence of territories the government may at any time resume.

questions.stem: Given the report, how does the company's force bear on the public purse?

options.text: At present it does not, since the company funds it, though the obligation survives if territories return
It does not, because the company has always refused any obligation of defence
options.misconception: invents a refusal of obligation

options.text: It does, because the company has charged the cost of its armies to the government since 1813
options.misconception: inverts who has paid since 1813

options.text: It does, because the cost of the armies has always exceeded the revenues of the territories
options.misconception: contradicts the report on the revenues

questions.explanation: The report says the company's revenues covered its armies, so no call on the public was made, while an obligation of defence would revive if territories were resumed. The alternatives invert the payment or deny the obligation.
questions.hint: Ask what would happen if the territories returned.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A fort that priced a river instead of closing it
questions.learningObjective: Compare a tolling fortress with a closing fortress
questions.stem: A seminar compares a river fortress that tolled passage with a strait fortress that closed it. Compare what each did for the trade that used the water.

options.text: The tolling fort enriched the ruler and the closing fort enriched the merchants who went around
options.misconception: claims closure enriched merchants

options.text: The tolling fort kept the trade in the ruler's hands and the closing fort drove it into another power's hands
options.misconception: mixes up the two cases

options.text: Both forts kept trade moving, one by price and one by escorting ships through under guard
options.misconception: invents an escort function

options.text: The tolling fort drew the trade to its own bank, while the closing fort pushed it away to rival ports

questions.explanation: A toll-taking fort drew shipping to its own quays and taxed it, whereas a closing fort diverted the trade to rivals. The alternatives merge the cases or invent functions such as escorting.
questions.hint: Ask where the ships went in each case.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two vocabularies for one exchange at a frontier
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a shared interpreting channel implied
questions.stem: A diplomatic arrangement required that negotiations be conducted through interpreters drawn from two languages and two legal traditions. What does that arrangement imply about the exchange?

options.text: That the two sides shared a common language, so no translation was in fact required
options.misconception: contradicts the arrangement

options.text: That each side was bound to accept whatever the interpreter said in the other's tongue
options.misconception: invents a binding rule about interpretation

options.text: That each side kept its own terms, and the shared channel was itself a point of dispute
That the exchange was conducted in the language of whichever side had the stronger army
options.misconception: invents a rule based on military strength

questions.explanation: Two languages and two traditions meant the terms lived in two systems, and the interpreter became a point of contest. The alternatives erase the difference or make interpretation automatic.
questions.hint: Ask who was trusted to translate.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: How coaling stations set a fleet's reach
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a coaling station became a strategic asset
questions.stem: Explain how a coaling station became a reason for a state to want a particular harbour, and how that changed the calculation of naval strategy.

answer.exemplar: A fleet could not remain at sea without somewhere to fill its bunkers, so a harbour with a depot was worth more than the same harbour without one: it was a place from which ships could operate in waters far from home, and its loss or its denial to an enemy could keep that enemy away from an entire sea. That gave harbour governments a reason to treat a coal wharf as a strategic asset, to garrison it, and to spend on it out of naval budgets, and it meant that a diplomatic dispute over a small stretch of coast could be settled in terms of fuel. The calculation changed from where ships could fight to where they could be supplied, and therefore to how far they had to be from their own bases.

questions.explanation: A depot made a harbour a base for distant operations, so states garrisoned and paid for coaling stations as strategy, not trade. Reading harbours as mattering only for shelter ignores the fuel supplied.
questions.hint: Ask what a warship needed most after ammunition.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a cable did to the distance between orders
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a wartime cable changed for a fleet

stimulus.body: The despatch reports that a line of telegraph has been laid between the fleet in the Baltic and the office in the city, and that the commanders in the squadrons are now able to receive instructions within a few hours instead of waiting for a ship to carry them. It adds that the enemy's position has changed twice in the interval between the despatch and its receipt.

questions.stem: According to the despatch, what did the line change?

options.text: The chain of command, since orders now travelled directly from the capital to each ship
options.misconception: claims the command structure itself changed

options.text: The time between an order being sent and being acted on, which the shifting enemy made decisive
The number of officers required to carry despatches between the squadrons
options.misconception: makes the change one of staffing

options.text: The enemy's ability to learn the position of the fleet, which the line now exposed
options.misconception: invents an interception

questions.explanation: The despatch values the line because it compressed the interval between a decision and the fleet's obedience. The alternatives relocate the change in command, staffing or secrecy.
questions.hint: Ask what the enemy did while the despatch travelled.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a prophylactic changed about the campaigning season
questions.learningObjective: Draw conclusions from a public works return

stimulus.body: The return shows that a tract of low ground in the neighbourhood of the town has been drained and levelled, that standing water has been cleared from the irrigation channels on a standing schedule, and that the returns of fever among the European and Egyptian population fell by more than half in the two seasons following the works.

questions.stem: Given the returns, what does the programme show about the campaigning season?

options.text: That the season was lengthened only for European troops, and not for the local population
options.misconception: restricts the effect to one group

options.text: That the works reduced the fever enough for the season to be worked throughout the year
That the drain and the clearing of channels removed the breeding places of the insect
options.misconception: confuses the means with the effect on the season

options.text: That the fall in fever resulted from the works alone, with no change in the insect population
options.misconception: credits the works without the insect

questions.explanation: The fall in fever across the whole population after the works changed the months the season could be worked, which is how the season lengthened. The alternatives restrict the effect or confuse the means with the effect.
questions.hint: Ask what the season could now do.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a defensive weapon changed the value of ground
questions.learningObjective: Assess the long-run consequences of a rising value of ground
questions.stem: A course asks how a defensive weapon changed the value of ground and then what followed from that change for the armies that fought in its shadow.

options.text: Ground became cheap again, and armies could manoeuvre freely as they had before the weapon appeared
options.misconception: reverses the change in the value of ground

options.text: Ground became worthless, so that no position was worth holding and campaigns grew short
options.misconception: overstates the consequence for campaigns

options.text: Nothing changed, since armies always preferred manoeuvre to the holding of positions
options.misconception: denies any change in practice

options.text: Ground became dear, so armies dug in, dispersed and turned the country into the weapon's weakness

questions.explanation: When ground grew dear, the response was to hold it, deny the enemy the open approaches and use the country against the attacker. The alternatives reverse the change or deny it.
questions.hint: Ask what the country could be used for.
